articles.title: Flight from reality
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S ruling elites devote inordinate time and attention to foreign engagements — at the expense of tackling domestic challenges. The country’s media also tends to focus more on foreign policy and international events than on fundamental problems confronting the country. Switch on any TV channel and most talk shows are endlessly discussing Pakistan’s overseas forays, defence agreements, and other global developments. Some of this is understandable as a war in the neighbourhood and regional and international dynamics do have implications for Pakistan that merit comment. But domestic issues more consequential to the country’s fate and future rarely receive the same attention. There may be several reasons for this. For ruling elites, foreign engagements are a way to access and collect geopolitical rents to keep the economy afloat, enabling them to avoid undertaking domestic reform. Their notion of ‘success’ rests on foreign alignments that can deliver these rents without having to expend political energy solving structural economic problems at home. Hence, the almost obsessive focus on foreign pursuits and lack of reform at home. For governments resting on dubious electoral mandates, it is also the means to acquire international legitimacy to compensate for its absence at home. This is more so for authoritarian and hybrid regimes. There is also more cachet in taking overseas trips and having photo-ops with world leaders than trying to get ministries to do their job. That is why ministers often spend more time abroad than in the country, with prime ministers exceeding their predecessors’ record of foreign visits. Fixing the country’s problems is much harder than flying off to, say, Davos. A cynical explanation is that the country’s problems — poverty, hunger, lack of education, and health facilities, malnutrition, growing population numbers — don’t affect the power elite, so if they fester there is no skin off its back. Certainly, it sees no urgency in addressing them. Pakistan’s future will be determined at home, not abroad. The excessive attention that much of Pakistan’s broadcast media devotes to foreign policy and external developments is explained by other factors. The obvious one is the electronic media simply covers what the country’s leadership is doing. But it also means it is content to play follow-my-leader and not set its own agenda that takes public issues into account. Discussing foreign trips and events involves far less effort than delving into complex domestic issues. Confrontations between the government and opposition do get plenty of coverage. But when a report on an aspect of Pakistan’s economic and social situation is published, the coverage and discussion are fleeting and shallow, with no analysis or follow-up. There are occasional exceptions but an in-depth analysis or investigative documentary on a consequential socioeconomic issue is hard to come by. Above all, TV channels seem to believe serving up formulaic talk shows is enough for viewers. Yet issues that warrant the attention of primarily the government, that can do something about them, and media, which can encourage authorities to pay attention, have become even more urgent. Improving the living conditions of people is the government’s most important task. That it has not lived up to this task is apparent from the fact that poverty, for example, has risen significantly in recent years. According to the World Bank, Pakistan’snational poverty rate rosefrom 22 per cent in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25. The WB also estimates that Pakistan accounts for almost half of the poor in the 23 countries of the MENAAP region (Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan). UNDP estimates 38.3pc of Pakistan’s population face multidimensional poverty, which measures multiple, overlapping deprivations in education, health, and standard of living that go beyond a purely monetary standard of poverty. So why is the government unable to deal with the increasing number of people living below the poverty line? It is argued that the government is constrained by the macroeconomic situation and an IMF programme that is contractionary, and has to focus on stabilising the economy. But that should not prevent it from addressing poverty. There is much that can be done to reduce poverty that has nothing to do with the spending cycle. After all, the IMF hardly prevents the government from allocating resources judiciously, mobilising revenue, pursuing non-tax filers, and curbing electricity theft. Stabilising the economy has nothing to do with vanity projects undertaken at the expense of helping the poor. Poverty is also reflected in the alarming state of hunger in the country. Pakistan is among the world’s 10 countries where millions face acute hunger, according to an international humanitarian organisation, Action Against Hunger. Another recent report, No Security Without Food Security,findsPakistan is worst hit by hunger in South Asia. Deteriorating food insecurity is attributed to economic instability, inflation, and climate shocks. Malnutrition associated with poverty is also responsible for child stunting. Around 40pc of Pakistani children under five are stunted, which condemns them to a life of physical disability, poverty, and lifelong deprivation. No issue matters more to the country’s future than education. Yet it barely gets priority attention from the government. Pakistan still has the world’s second highest number of out-of-school children, around 25m (aged five to 16) — over half of them girls. This is a national scandal. Literacy remains stagnant, with 37pc of people illiterate. No country can make economic progress with that level of illiteracy. Without investment in people, economic growth will remain elusive. The education deficit is all the more serious given the youth bulge. Over two-thirds of the population are below age 30. The young will determine the country’s destiny. But if they are uneducated and unemployable, they face a hopeless future. This jeopardises the country’s prospects. Also disturbing is the share of youth (15-29 years) who are not in education, employment, and training, known as the NEET rate, which is 37pc overall and 62pc for women, according to a Gallup report. Human capital and human development, crucial for economic growth, have suffered from government indifference and deteriorated over time. Foreign engagements count for little when there is no improvement in the condition of the majority of people. Nor does the ‘glamour’ of foreign trips obscure the grim reality of the economic and social deprivations people face across the country. Nation-building at home should have priority. Pakistan’s future, after all, will be determined at home, not abroad. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: A shifting cycle
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S 2024 election results marked the end of a political cycle that began in the early 2000s. Less often noted is that this cycle expired at roughly the same moment as the global order which framed it. Signs of political and cultural realignment are now fully emergent, and their trajectory passes through events of the past 25 years — the ‘war on terror’ and its effects on Muslim societies, the financial crisis alongside growth in Asian economies, and increased migration to Western countries. The Pakistani domestic cycle is best characterised as an unsuccessful attempt to achieve a political settlement, under the garb of federalised (and electoral) constitutional rule. Its participants were the traditional parties PML-N and PPP, and their core constituents, sections of liberal civil society and private news media, and some segments of the judiciary. Its opposition came from entities excluded from or antagonised by that brief lived system of patronage: the PTI, the upwardly mobile urban classes, and the military establishment and its aligned factions among the media. The latter coalition won out over the last 10 years. In winning, it stumbled upon its own internal contradictions, which are now playing out as the present crisis. This cycle, however, was always nested inside something larger. Its vocabulary of rights, its civil society, and much of its international support came from a global dispensation; NGO work here was intellectually and financially sustained by Western aid largesse in the context of the war on terror. Once the external scaffolding weakened, the undoing at home proved swift. That scaffolding is what we commonly dub the neoliberal world order. Characterised by deregulation in markets, and trade and financial liberalisation, these prescriptions were macroeconomic orthodoxy for nearly four decades. They represented the response of the capitalist class to the stagflation crisis of the 1970s in Western economies, dismantling the political power of labour by making offshoring easier, and restoring the power of capital through financialisation. The recipe would remain incomplete without access to new labour, product, and capital markets, which is why it came packaged as IMF-run ‘structural adjustment’ for countries in the Global South. The Pakistani domestic cycle is best characterised as an unsuccessful attempt to achieve a political settlement. What did these four decades of liberalisation deliver? Growth for some countries (East Asia, parts of Latin America), stagnation and deindustrialisation for most others, astronomical returns for owners of finance capital, and heightened inequality nearly everywhere. Since 2008, populations in the West have rightly soured on this misfiring orthodoxy, and that resentment has gradually made its way into how decision-makers think about their economies. Free markets are no longer considered orthodoxy (at least in rhetoric). The unravelling of the old order extends beyond economics. Liberal democracy was presented as a core value, supposedly maintained by the US globally. Its use as a cynical foreign policy stick had already made many in the world wary. Elsewhere, the appeal of some authoritarian systems is growing. Sociologist Cihan Tugal points to Turkiye under Erdogan and the AKP, which has used state welfare, economic intervention, and centralised politics to contain opposition over two decades. Key political and establishment figures in countries like Pakistan now routinely view limits on democracy as necessary for economic progress. Does this reordering then offer Pakistan an opening? Statist nationalists see the country’s expanded role in regional geopolitical affairs as both a vindication of its military-led governing structure and a route to its destined status as a regional power. On the face of it, both shifts work in the country’s favour. As a state with strong military capabilities, both nuclear and conventional, Pakistan can extract material concessions from regional powers looking for a security patron after the US winds down its position. And for a countrylong locked into IMF programmes, escaping some elements of neoliberal economic orthodoxy is a necessity. The real question is: can it? Here the answer goes back to how the global is refracted into the local via the domestic arrangements that actually exist on the ground. Can the rentier/ patronage economy be turned productive? Can those with outsized claims on the exchequer be reined in? The task rests with a state overwhelmed by a military-bureaucratic establishment that has turned its primary logic into one of extraction via authoritarian decree rather than service delivery. More importantly, this is a state of viceregal origin, incapable of the mass mobilisation and disciplining that engendered effective capacity in Korea or China. It is held together instead by the distribution of rents, internally to its cadres and kin, and externally to a narrow sliver of the population. The traditional parties that might have steered this moment have proven completely unable to do so. Their mode of politics rested on narrow patronage relations with socially dominant segments in Punjab and Sindh, and in exchange for temporary respite they outsourced Fata, Balochistan, judicial independence, electoral competition, and even large parts of governance to the militarised logic of establishment control. Most of all, they have ignored the emergent reality of the upwardly mobile, digitally resourceful urban middle classes and inflation-weary masses, leaving the field wide open for multiple types of resentment. However, resentment on its own is insufficient to lead society anywhere. The arduous task for those still committed to broad-based material uplift lies in reworking the state into something attentive to the collective good and capable of mobilising society for it. This is not a reworking that will be handed to progressives with any ease. In fact, in the absence of viable progressive movements to project some notion of universal justice, the militarisation of the region and the turn to narrow, sectional resentment is a recipe for further marginalisation of the already vulnerable. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: COP31 arrives
articles.content: WHEN leaders gather in Antalya for COP31, the formal agenda will be familiar: emissions, adaptation, climate finance, technology, and implementation. Yet the significance of this conference may lie beyond any individual negotiating text. COP31 arrives 10 years after the Paris Agreement, at a moment when the world that produced Paris has changed profoundly. In 2015, multilateralism still carried considerable confidence. Globalisation appeared broadly irreversible; economic interdependence was viewed more as a stabilising force than a strategic vulnerability; technological change was promising transformation but had not yet become a source of geopolitical rivalry. Today, wars, strategic competition, fractured supply chains, industrial policy and technological disruption have altered the international landscape. Climate change itself has become more immediate, while the clean-energy transition has become an arena of economic and strategic competition. Paris succeeded in establishing a common framework in which every country accepted responsibility for contributing to the climate response, while recognising differences in circumstances and capabilities. The question before Antalya will, therefore, not be whether to move beyond Paris, but how to make its promise workable in the world that has emerged since it was signed. At a time when geopolitical tensions are shrinking space for climate cooperation and 1.5 degrees Celsius overshoot is imminent, the environmental imperative is becoming harder to separate from questions of security and development. The bigger challenge will be how to steer a complex agenda with fragmented cooperation to make COP and the UNFCCC process fit for this era. This creates both an opportunity and a dilemma. Countries need one another to address a planetary problem, even as they compete for technologies, markets, minerals, manufacturing capacity, and strategic influence. Antalya is an occasion to ask a question larger than climate policy. The conference has already been conceived as an implementation-oriented COP, with priorities encompassing energy transition, resilient infrastructure, green industry, agriculture, finance, and vulnerable regions. But climate negotiations cannot carry this burden alone. The deeper question is whether the institutional architecture of international cooperation remains adequate to address the problems of this century. The Bretton Woods institutions were created in the aftermath of World War II to address the monetary, financial, and reconstruction challenges of their time. The United Nations system emerged from the same historical moment. Those institutions remain essential, but the distribution of economic power, technology and population has changed dramatically. The developing world now calls for more than incremental reform. It calls for a new conversation between climate diplomacy and global economic governance. The same is true of technology. AI, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, digital systems, and new energy technologies are developing at extraordinary speed. They offer tools for climate adaptation, scientific discovery, efficient energy systems, and better resource management. Yet access to these capabilities is becoming uneven, and technological dependence can itself become a source of strategic vulnerability. The international community, therefore, needs institutions capable not merely of regulating yesterday’s risks but of governing emerging technologies, facilitating their responsible diffusion and ensuring that technological progress does not deepen existing inequalities. This is where the climate negotiations can become a catalyst COP31 should remain firmly anchored in the UN climate process and the Paris Agreement. But it can also begin connecting climate action with the wider architecture of finance, technology, trade, energy, and development. The world does not need to choose between multilateralism and national interest. A durable international order must recognise that responsible national interest increasingly depends upon functioning global cooperation. Antalya, therefore, offers an opportunity to ask a question that is larger than climate policy: what kind of international system is required for a century defined simultaneously by planetary limits, technological acceleration, and geopolitical plurality? The answer will not be found in a single summit. But COP31 can help begin the conversation. Paris gave the world a climate framework. The task now is to build the economic, technological, and political architecture capable of delivering it. The UNFCCC will remain the universal forum for climate cooperation but it will need to adapt to meet the demands of the century that is unfolding. COP31 can serve as a bridge to build the order we now need.
articles.author: Aisha Khan

articles.title: Nuclear arc
articles.content: LAST week, Iranian state media broadcast instructions on how citizens could stay safe in the event of a nuclear strike. The broadcast covered what people should do if caught in an atomic flash, tips on decontaminating clothes, and what families should keep ready in a ‘nuclear emergency bag’. In the midst of a spiralling regional conflict, this dystopian broadcast is a chilling reminder of how much worse it could get — and so, of how urgently de-escalation is required, particularly as the US and Israel enter a period of political uncertainty following respective elections. De-escalation efforts are underway, with Qatar reportedly pushing hard for a negotiated end to the conflict. These negotiations hinge on Iran agreeing to reopen its nuclear programme to inspections and accepting curbs on enrichment levels in exchange for US sanctions relief. Such a negotiated end would be very welcome, given how the spectre of nuclear conflict increasingly haunts the Middle East. One factor that could influence the way this de-escalation proceeds is how the US Congress, freshly stuffed with Democrats, may tackle the US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement reached this summer. The agreement for civilian nuclear cooperation paves the way for the US transferring technology to Saudi Arabia that would enable it to enrich uranium for nuclear energy production within the kingdom. This would be an exceptional agreement because, as Robert Einhorn points out in a brief for Brookings, Washington typically opposes the spread of fuel-cycle capabilities to new countries. When announced, the deal rang alarm bells for nuclear non-proliferation experts because it does not require Saudi Arabia to adhere to the IAEA’s Additional Protocol, the legal mechanism which enables the IAEA to check for illicit weapons production. The kingdom refused to sign up to the AP on the basis that potential inspections around holy sites would be too sensitive. This, critics of the deal say, opens a loophole through which Saudi Arabia could divert enriched uranium for weapons production at undeclared sites — an uncomfortable scenario given that Riyadh has stated it would pursue weapons production if Iran acquired nuclear weapons. The US-Saudi civilian nuclear pact will impact Iran’s strategy. The Trump administration is willing to proceed with the deal for the following reasons: the civilian nuclear technology transfer will be governed by a Bilateral Safeguards Agreement, which will allow for inspection and monitoring of all declared sites. The US also envisions an exclusive arrangement with Saudi Arabia, meaning the latter would be locked into a ‘black box’ of US-supplied nuclear know-how, technology and equipment, enabling Washington to closely manage Saudi Arabia’s nuclear capability and production. Finally, Washington has reasoned that if it doesn’t reach an agreement with Riyadh, then Moscow or Beijing will instead, and those deals would inevitably have even fewer protections against nuclear weapons proliferation. The agreement, currently pending with the Congress, would take effect in mid-December if not proactively blocked (an unlikely scenario given congressional priorities, a likely presidential veto of any block, and cross-party appetite to repair ties with Riyadh). But greater Democratic heft may temper the agreement, including renewed efforts to get Saudi Arabia to agree to the AP, limits on the transfer of sensitive enrichment technology, curbs on data sharing, and enhanced reporting on Riyadh’s compliance with non-proliferation terms to Congress. In all scenarios, the US-Saudi civilian nuclear pact, and the proliferation risks it is perceived to en- tail, will influence Iran’s approach to conflict resolution, potentially stymying progress on curtailing Tehran’s nuclear am-bitions. The prospect — howe- ver distant — of a nuclear-armed Saudi Arabia in addition to Israel is unlikely to inspire Tehran to disarmament. It will also create regional appetite for more civilian nuclear deals with less adherence to the AP and more localisation of uranium enrichment. Turkey, for example, which has civilian nuclear cooperation deals with the US, Russia, and China, or the UAE, which has an existing agreement with the US that disallows uranium enrichment, may seek technology transfer to enable enrichment and reprocessing within their borders. What are the security implications of a Middle East with varying degrees of enrichment capabilities subject to different inspections regimes? The idea is concerning, and requires sensible controls and scenario planning to prevent rampant proliferation. Above all, it requires trust among regional actors that civilian nuclear capability will not be repurposed for weapons production. Sadly, the mere potential for proliferation will exacerbate, not ease, the regional trust deficit. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: Antalya agenda
articles.content: WHEN COP31 opens in Antalya today, governments will have to show that years of climate negotiations have produced more than ambitious targets and promises of financial help. Geopolitical tensions, an energy crisis, and strained finances in rich countries have dampened hopes of a breakthrough. The absence of an official US delegation after Washington’swithdrawal from the Paris Agreementhas worsened matters. Meanwhile, the climate crisis is advancing faster than efforts to contain it. A new UN reportwarnsthat even if countries fulfil existing climate pledges, global temperatures could rise by 2.6°C this century. For Pakistan, already exposed to floods, extreme heat, and erratic rainfall, the question is what it can realistically secure from the talks. At COP29, developed countriescommittedto mobilising $300bn annually for developing nations by 2035. COP30 called for progress towards a broader goal of $1.3tr a year and for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035. But promises of more money mean little if vulnerable states cannot access it. For Pakistan, the priority should be to secure easier access to climate funds, more grants rather than debt-creating loans, and clear deadlines for financial contributions. It should seek support for practical measures to protect homes from flooding, secure water supplies, and improve early warning systems. By joining forces with other vulnerable countries, Pakistan could strengthen calls for better glacier monitoring, flood protection, and affordable climate technology. Its latest climate plan aims to cut projected emissions by 50pc by 2035, with 17 percentage points unconditional and the remaining 33 reliant on international support. This gives Pakistan grounds to seek investment in cleaner energy, transport, and agriculture. But it must also pursue reforms at home, while pressing for stronger global action to reduce emissions. Pakistan’s preparations for COP31 offer an opportunity to put these priorities into practice. Its planned pavilion sessions in Antalya cover disaster preparedness, solar electrification, local adaptation, and climate investment projects. These discussions should lead to partnerships and investment proposals. Islamabad should identify priority projects and report publicly on commitments secured and money received. Provincial governments must be involved, as irrigation, land use, drainage, and emergency services are largely their responsibility. Local communities should help determine which projects receive priority funding. Pakistan must also address problems that international aid alone cannot solve, including construction on floodplains and poor enforcement of environmental rules. COP31 may produce modest advances rather than a sweeping agreement. But Pakistan can still make progress by presenting workable proposals and showing that the assistance it receives will benefit those most at risk.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Beyond viewership
articles.content: PAKISTAN has an enormous appetite for online content. According to the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority, it leads the world in daily YouTube viewership, with 96m users watching 560m videos a day. TikTok and WhatsApp command similarly vast audiences. And yet millions of Pakistanis struggle with slow connections, patchy mobile coverage, and unreliable service. A video may load eventually, but a student attending a virtual class or a small business processing a payment cannot afford interruptions. The government should, therefore, measure digital progress by whether people can depend on the internet to learn, work, and earn, rather than by the number of accounts opened or videos watched. In smaller towns and rural areas, adequate coverage remains elusive, deepening inequalities between citizens who can access opportunities online and those who cannot. Even in major cities, users complain of poor service. The expansion of 5G to selected cities is welcome, but it means little to those struggling with basic connectivity. Investment in fibre networks, wider coverage, and network maintenance must be matched with affordable packages and meaningful regulatory oversight. Operators should be held to measurable service standards, while arbitrary curbs that disrupt communications and business must end. Infrastructure alone, however, will not create a digitally capable society. Pakistan’s extraordinary social media consumption tells us little about how confidently its citizens can navigate the online world. Many users remain vulnerable to scams, identity theft, and the misuse of personal information. Others lack the skills to apply digital tools to education and employment. Digital literacy must become a priority, beginning in schools and extending through colleges, vocational institutes, and training centres. Lessons must go beyond operating smartphones to cover online safety, fact-checking, privacy, digital payments, and responsible AI use. Special efforts are needed to reach women, older citizens, and rural populations. Public institutions could work with telecom companies, educators, and civil society to offer practical instruction in local languages. Such programmes would help turn passive consumption into useful participation in the digital economy. Pakistan has no shortage of people willing to go online. What it lacks is a reliable network and a broad base of skills to make that access worthwhile.
articles.author: Editorial
